frameworks.name: Two Signs of Future Wealth
frameworks.definition: A framework identifying wealth trajectory through two measurable indicators: monetary measuring units (base unit size for money-denominated decisions) and time horizon (speed of execution and duration of goal commitment).

frameworks.name: Measuring Sticks
frameworks.definition: The cognitive shorthand units (e.g., Chipotle burritos, $1K, $10K, $1M) that people use to mentally chunk and evaluate financial decisions; larger units correlate with wealth and determine participation in opportunities.

frameworks.name: Time Perspective Axis (Micro and Macro)
frameworks.definition: Two dimensions of time-based decision-making: micro (daily execution speed and communication turnaround) and macro (time horizon in years/decades for goal achievement).

claims.text: The size of a person's monetary measuring unit predicts their wealth trajectory. People who habitually measure money in larger base units (e.g., $100K chunks instead of $1K chunks) participate in higher-leverage opportunities and accumulate wealth faster, because activities below their unit threshold feel not worth doing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Larger monetary units create a psychological floor below which activities feel unworthy; thus the person naturally filters for high-leverage opportunities, while someone with a $1K unit participates in $100 activities that compound into distraction.

claims.text: Wealthy people teach their children to pursue opportunities measured in larger monetary units and to pursue higher-leverage activities, while less wealthy parents do not instill this filter.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Wealthy parents model and reinforce larger monetary measuring units, conditioning children to filter opportunities by size; less wealthy parents do not provide this frame.

claims.text: Micro-level execution speed (how fast someone communicates, responds, and closes loops) is a visible marker of wealth. A person who responds within hours instead of days demonstrates higher time leverage and will accomplish far more in a given calendar period.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fast turnaround time on back-and-forth exchanges compresses the calendar time needed to complete projects; fast operators accomplish in a day what slow operators take a month for, due to parallel compression of sequential back-and-forths.

numbers.axis: project completion time via communication speed

claims.text: Changing the default completion deadline from end-of-week to end-of-day (or 4 hours from now) is a macro time-measuring-stick shift that increases overall velocity. The tighter the deadline default, the faster an organization executes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when default deadlines are explicit and non-negotiable
claims.mechanism: Explicit shorter-horizon defaults compress decision cycles and force prioritization; teams operating to end-of-day defaults parallelize and compress work that end-of-week teams spread across the week.

claims.text: The willingness to wait years or decades to achieve a goal (macro time horizon) is a key predictor of wealth and success. People who can delay gratification and think in decade-long time horizons compound their efforts far more effectively than people who think in days or weeks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Long time horizons enable sustained effort on compound-returning activities (e.g., building reputation, infrastructure) that short-horizon thinkers abandon because they don't see returns within weeks; impulse control (self-restraint) enables the delayed gratification required for long-horizon compounding.

claims.text: The marshmallow test (one immediate reward vs. two delayed rewards) predicts lifetime success: children who delay gratification and wait for the larger reward become significantly wealthier and more successful than children who demand immediate payoff.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Extending the marshmallow test delay further (1 hour, 1 day, 1 week, 1 year) increases the success gap: the person who can wait the longest (largest time delta before gratification) will be significantly more successful than those who demand faster payoff.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Success compounds over long periods because sustained effort on unrewarded work (short-term) produces exponential returns (long-term); only people with extended gratification horizons can sustain that effort.

numbers.axis: delay-to-reward period in the extended marshmallow test

claims.text: Surrounding yourself with people who use larger monetary measuring units, shorter micro-execution cycles, and decade-long time horizons will accelerate your own wealth accumulation and goal achievement compared to staying in peer groups with smaller units and shorter horizons.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Peer groups establish cognitive defaults through modeling and implicit standard-setting; hanging with people who use $1M units shifts your own reference frame upward, just as hanging with fast executors compresses your cycles. Your brain adapts to the group's baseline.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi used Chipotle burrito units ($8-10 each, estimated) as his measuring stick when in high school because that was the amount of money he earned and perceived as a meaningful unit of value. As he accumulated wealth, he shifted his unit to $10K, then $100K, then million-dollar units (which hedge funds call a 'stick'). This progression forced him to evaluate opportunities only in terms of how many 'sticks' they generated, naturally filtering out small-value activities.

In a project where two people need five back-and-forth exchanges: a slow-responder pair takes 10 days (1 day per person per exchange), while a fast-responder pair completes all five exchanges in 30 minutes. Over months, the fast pair compounds this speed advantage: in a month, they accomplish what the slow pair takes several months to finish.

A conversation between Alex Hormozi and a friend who exited his company for just under half a billion dollars formed the basis for this framework. The friend identified two key patterns in successful people he had observed: their relationship to measuring sticks around money and time.

practices.text: Increase the base unit of money you measure things in, starting with awareness of your current unit and intentionally shifting to the next higher tier (e.g., $1K → $10K → $100K).
Change your organizational default deadline from end-of-week to end-of-day (or even 4 hours from now) to compress execution cycles.
Intentionally hang around people who use larger monetary units, execute faster, and think in decade-long time horizons; allow their defaults to become your new baselines.
Practice delayed gratification and self-restraint on small decisions; build the impulse-control muscle that enables long-horizon goal setting.
